name: Charitable Remainder Trust for Appreciated Assets

advisor.summary: A §664 charitable remainder trust converts a low-basis appreciated asset into a payout stream without a taxable sale: the donor funds the trust, the tax-exempt trust sells and reinvests the full pre-tax proceeds, and the deferred gain flows back out over the term through the four-tier distribution ordering. The donor takes a current deduction equal to the actuarial value of the charitable remainder, which must clear the 10% test, and the charity receives what is left at the end. Nothing here eliminates the gain — it is spread, often across decades and often at lower stacked rates than a lump-sum year. The transaction the IRS actually wins is the mistimed one: fund after the buyer is effectively locked in and assignment-of-income doctrine puts the whole gain back on the donor. This is an advisory record — the engine does not model CRT economics, and every number presented to a client must come from dedicated actuarial software.
mechanics: The trust is exempt from income tax under §664(c), so it sells the contributed asset without current gain and reinvests the entire pre-tax proceeds; the donor's gain is deferred into the payout stream rather than erased.

Distributions are taxed worst-in, first-out through the §664(b) four tiers — ordinary income first, then capital gain, then other income, then tax-free corpus — so the trapped appreciation typically emerges as tier-two capital gain spread over many years, and the trustee's investment policy controls which tier each payment carries.

Design choice: a unitrust (CRUT) pays a fixed percentage of annually revalued assets, between 5% and 50%, and accepts later additions; an annuity trust (CRAT) pays a fixed dollar amount, allows no additions, and must survive the exhaustion test. CRUTs dominate in practice.

The donor's deduction under §170(f)(2)(A) equals the actuarial value of the charitable remainder computed at the §7520 rate; the remainder must be at least 10% of the funding value under §664(d), and gifts of appreciated long-term property run through the 30%-of-AGI ceiling of §170(b)(1)(C) with a five-year carryforward.

Sequence is everything: the trust must own the asset before any binding sale obligation exists. Rev. Rul. 78-197 draws the line — gain is taxed to the donor where the donee is legally bound, or can be compelled, to complete the sale at the time of the gift — and the negotiation posture at funding must be documented in the file.

The trust files Form 5227 annually and the four-tier character of each distribution flows to the income beneficiary on a Schedule K-1; a wealth-replacement life insurance trust is the customary pairing when heirs must be made whole for the remainder passing to charity.

authority.note: The CRT regime: qualification, the 5%–50% payout corridor, the four-tier distribution ordering of §664(b), the trust's exemption under §664(c), and the 10% minimum-remainder tests of §664(d).
The deduction is limited to the remainder interest's actuarial value, and appreciated-property gifts are capped at 30% of AGI with a five-year carryforward.
The actuarial rate used to value the remainder — the rate environment materially moves both the deduction and 10%-test feasibility.
The assignment-of-income bright line: gain lands on the donor where the trust is legally bound to sell at the time of the gift.
Donors taxed on gain where stock was contributed after a tender offer had made the sale practically certain — the case examiners reach for when funding follows the deal.
The split-interest trust annual information return; the four-tier accounts and beneficiary K-1 reporting live here.

requirements: A highly appreciated, salable asset free of complications — low-basis securities or unmortgaged real estate; debt-financed property creates UBTI exposure inside the trust.
Funding completed before any binding sale obligation exists, with the state of negotiations memorialized in writing at the contribution date.
A payout design that lands between 5% and 50% and produces an actuarial remainder of at least 10% of contributed value at the current §7520 rate.
Genuine charitable intent — the remainder is real money that leaves the family.
A trustee arrangement capable of annual valuations, four-tier accounting, and Form 5227 compliance for the life of the trust.
risks: Anticipatory assignment of income is the leading audit theory: Ferguson v. Commissioner, 174 F.3d 997 (9th Cir. 1999) put the gain back on donors who funded after the sale was practically certain, and Rev. Rul. 78-197 supplies the government's bright line. Funding-date documentation is the whole defense.
The trust is irrevocable — changed family circumstances cannot unwind it, and only the payout stream remains accessible.
Qualification can fail at drafting: a payout rate that flunks the 10% remainder test, or a CRAT that fails the exhaustion test, means no deduction and a fully taxable sale.
UBTI — including debt-financed income from mortgaged property — draws a 100% excise tax on that income; encumbered real estate must be restructured before contribution.
The tier-one trap: a trustee who invests for ordinary income forces distributions to carry out ordinary income first, converting a capital-gain deferral into ordinary-rate payouts.
stateNotes: States that conform to federal AGI pick up the four-tier character of distributions automatically, but state treatment of the charitable deduction varies — verify the deduction's state value separately in states with their own itemized regimes.
No PTET interaction — this is individual charitable and capital-gain planning with no entity-level election in play.

Missouri conforms through its federal-AGI starting point (RSMo §143.121), and under the 2025 capital-gains legislation (RSMo §143.121, HB 594) individuals subtract 100% of federally reported capital gains — so tier-two capital-gain distributions should escape Missouri tax as well; confirm the subtraction's application to K-1 character when the first payout year is filed.
reviewChecklist: No binding sale obligation exists at funding, and the negotiation posture is memorialized in the file with dates.
The payout design clears the 10% remainder test (and the CRAT exhaustion test if applicable) at the current §7520 rate.
The deduction is modeled against the 30%-of-AGI ceiling with a carryforward schedule the client has seen.
Estate counsel is engaged for drafting, and a qualified appraisal is ordered for any non-marketable asset.
The client has acknowledged in writing that the trust is irrevocable and the remainder genuinely passes to charity.
Wealth-replacement insurance has been considered and priced where heirs need to be made whole.

client.teaser: Sell a big winner with no tax due at the sale — and get paid from it for life.
client.headline: Turn one big gain into income for life and a gift you choose
plainEnglish: Selling an asset that has grown for years usually hands a large slice to the IRS first. A charitable remainder trust changes the order. You give the asset to a trust you set up. The trust sells it and pays no tax on the sale. Every dollar goes back to work for you.

The trust then pays you each year, for life or for a set term. You pay tax on those payments as they arrive, spread over many years. You also get a charitable deduction in the year you fund the trust.

When the trust ends, what remains goes to a charity you pick. Many families use part of the income to buy life insurance so the kids receive full value too. One thing matters most: the trust must own the asset before any sale is locked in.
client.analogy: It is like donating an orchard to a foundation that pays you from every future harvest. The trees never stop working for you, and the tax bill on selling the orchard never lands.
benefits: No tax at the sale, so the full value is reinvested for you
Dependable payments for life or a term you choose
A charitable deduction in the year you fund the trust
A real gift to a cause you care about, with options to keep heirs whole
steps: WE model the income stream, the deduction, and the tax result next to a plain sale.
WE coordinate the estate attorney who drafts the trust and the appraiser if one is needed.
YOU fund the trust before any sale agreement is signed.
WE handle the trust's annual filings and your tax reporting every year after.
clientCommitments: Bring us in before you talk price with any buyer — funding must come first
Accept that the gift is permanent; the asset cannot come back to you
Keep the trustee's paperwork and annual filings on schedule

annualMaintenance: Form 5227 preparation and beneficiary K-1 issuance each year
Four-tier account tracking and annual asset revaluation for unitrust payouts
Investment-policy review against the tier ordering so payouts keep their intended character
deliverables: CRT design memo — CRAT vs. CRUT, payout rate, and the deduction at the current §7520 rate
Funding-sequence checklist with negotiation-status documentation for the file
Annual Form 5227 package with the four-tier accounting schedule

suggest.reason: A CRT spreads a large gain over years while funding charity and an income stream.
